sermon:
## The Glory by the River Chebar
*God finds the exiles where the temple cannot reach*

**Text:** Ezekiel 1–3 · **Supporting:** Psalm 137:1–4; Isaiah 6:1–8; Revelation 1:12–17; Jeremiah 29:4–7

The wheels do not appear in Jerusalem. They appear in Babylon. They appear by an irrigation ditch in the flat country of a foreign empire, four hundred miles from the only place where Israel believed God could be found, and that is the first sermon the book preaches before Ezekiel opens his mouth.

**The wrong address**
Everything in Israel's theology said the glory lived in one room. Behind the veil, over the ark, between the cherubim — that was the throne, and the throne did not travel. So when the deportation of 597 BC dragged a priest named Ezekiel into exile, it dragged him out of range. A priest with no temple is a man whose entire vocation has lost its address. The exiles by the Chebar canal had a theology that left them stranded, and they sat down by the water and wept (Psalm 137:1). Then the heavens opened over the wrong country. "As I looked, behold, a stormy wind came out of the north, and a great cloud, with brightness around it, and fire flashing forth continually" (Ezekiel 1:4). The God who could not leave Jerusalem came to Babylon. The throne had wheels.

**A vision that refuses to be domesticated**
Read the first chapter slowly and you will notice it resists you. Four living creatures, four faces each, wheels within wheels, eyes everywhere, a firmament like awful crystal, and above it a likeness of a throne and a likeness of a man and fire and brightness all around. Ezekiel does not describe God. He describes the appearance of the likeness of the glory, three words deep in qualifications, because the thing he saw cannot be flattened into a picture you could put over a couch. This is the same instinct as Isaiah, who saw the Lord high and lifted up and could only report the train of his robe filling the temple and the cry of holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:1–3). It is the same as John on Patmos, who saw the risen Christ and fell at his feet as though dead (Revelation 1:17). The honest response to the glory is not enthusiasm. It is the ground. "And when I saw it, I fell upon my face" (Ezekiel 1:28). The man face-down in the dirt is the man who saw clearly.

**Eat the scroll before you speak the word**
Then the commission, and it is not flattering. God does not send Ezekiel to a hungry crowd waiting for a word. He sends him to a rebellious house, to people of a hard forehead and a stubborn heart, and he tells the prophet in advance that they will not listen — and to go anyway. Before a single oracle, God hands him a scroll written on front and back with words of lamentation and mourning and woe, and says, "Son of man, eat this scroll that I give you and fill your stomach with it." And Ezekiel eats it, "and it was in my mouth as sweet as honey" (Ezekiel 3:3). The lament tastes sweet going down because the word of God is sweet even when its content is grief. But you cannot preach what you have not swallowed. The watchman has to digest the warning before he delivers it. He has to carry the weight in his own body before he sets it on anyone else.

And here is where the river Chebar stops being ancient history and turns around on us. We have built our own theology of God's address. We have decided where he can be found — in the building, in the music we like, in the season when things were working, in the country when it was ours. And when the deportation comes, when the marriage ends or the diagnosis lands or the church we built our identity on splits, we sit down by our own canal and conclude that God stayed behind in the place we lost. I have done this. I have grieved the absence of God in the exact moment he was opening the heavens over the wrong country to find me. The glory has wheels precisely so that it can come for the people who cannot come back. This is the whole logic of the gospel four centuries early — the God who will not stay in the holy place, who moves toward the unclean, who in Jesus Christ comes all the way out to where we are face-down in the dirt and lifts us by the Spirit to our feet. The exile did not put Ezekiel beyond God's reach. Nothing does.

God finds you in exile.

## The Watchman's Blood
*The terrible weight of the warning you were given to give*

**Text:** Ezekiel 3:16–27; 33:1–20 · **Supporting:** Acts 20:26–27; Ezekiel 18:23; James 3:1; Hebrews 13:17

The job description is the most frightening one in the Old Testament. Not because of what the watchman suffers, but because of who answers for the silence.

**The man on the wall**
A watchman stands on the city wall for one reason. He sees the sword coming before the city does, and he sounds the trumpet, and the warning gives the people a chance to live. God takes this image and lays it on Ezekiel directly. "Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel. Whenever you hear a word from my mouth, you shall give them warning from me" (Ezekiel 3:17). Then God draws the line that should keep every preacher awake. If the watchman sees the sword and does not blow the trumpet, and a man dies, "that person shall die for his iniquity, but his blood I will require at the watchman's hand" (Ezekiel 33:6). The man dies for his own sin. The watchman answers for the silence. Two deaths, two different charges, and the second one belongs to the man who knew and said nothing.

**The line the warning does not cross**
Now grant the objection, because it is a real one. This sounds like a system where the messenger is responsible for the choices of the hearer, and that is a crushing and unfair thing to lay on anyone. But read the text again, because Ezekiel is careful where we are sloppy. If the watchman does blow the trumpet and the people do not heed it, "his blood shall be upon his own head. But he who takes warning shall save his life" (Ezekiel 33:5). The watchman is not responsible for the response. He is responsible for the warning. The whole of chapter 18 stands behind this — every soul answers for its own life, the wicked who turns will live, and God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but rather that he turn and live (Ezekiel 18:23). The watchman cannot make a man turn. He can only refuse to let him die unwarned. That is the line, and it is exactly placed. You are not the savior. You are the trumpet.

**What we do with the trumpet**
Here is where it stops being about Ezekiel. We have learned to call our silence by gentler names. We call it not being pushy. We call it respecting where they are. We call it tone, and timing, and not wanting to make it weird, and every one of those names is sometimes true and sometimes the watchman setting down the trumpet because blowing it costs him something. I know this from the inside. I have softened the warning for someone I loved because I would rather keep the friendship comfortable than tell them the sword was coming, and I have called that wisdom when it was cowardice. Paul stood before the Ephesian elders and said, "I am innocent of the blood of all, for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God" (Acts 20:26–27). He could only say that because he had not edited the message down to what was welcome. James warns that teachers will be judged with greater strictness (James 3:1), and this is why. The man given the warning to give answers for the giving of it.

But the watchman points past himself. There is one Watchman who sounded every warning and was met with the very sword he warned of — who took the blood he was not required to take, ours, onto his own head at the cross. The shepherd-watchman of Hebrews keeps watch over our souls as one who must give an account (Hebrews 13:17), and he gave the fullest account love could give. So the call to warn is not a burden laid on us alone in the dark. It is participation in the mercy of a God who does not want the wicked to die, who put his own Son on the wall, and who hands us the trumpet not to crush us but because he genuinely does not want them to die unwarned. The cost of speaking is real. The cost of silence is someone's blood.

Warn them, or their blood answers.

## The Siege Acted Out
*When the prophet's own body becomes the sermon*

**Text:** Ezekiel 4–5 · **Supporting:** Jeremiah 19:1–11; Isaiah 20:2–4; Hosea 1:2–3; Ezekiel 12:11

By chapter four the words have not worked. So God stops telling Ezekiel to speak and starts telling him to perform, because there is a kind of numbness that only a picture can break.

**The brick and the iron pan**
The instructions are strange and concrete. Take a brick, scratch the city of Jerusalem on it, and lay siege to it — build a ramp, set up camps, place battering rams all around. Then take an iron griddle and set it as an iron wall between yourself and the city. "This is a sign for the house of Israel" (Ezekiel 4:3). Then lie on your left side three hundred ninety days for the iniquity of Israel, and on your right side forty days for Judah, bearing the punishment in your own body. Ration your bread and water and weigh it out by the shekel, eating bread cooked over a fire, because that is how men eat when the city is starving inside the wall. The prophets did this. Jeremiah smashed a clay jar in front of the elders and said this is how the city will be broken (Jeremiah 19:10–11). Isaiah walked naked and barefoot three years as a sign against Egypt (Isaiah 20:3). God married Hosea to an unfaithful woman so the man's own marriage would preach Israel's betrayal (Hosea 1:2). When the word stops landing, God makes the prophet's life the word.

**The hair divided into thirds**
Then the hardest sign of all. Take a sharp sword and shave your head and your beard, and weigh the hair and divide it into three parts. Burn a third in the fire inside the city. Strike a third with the sword around it. Scatter a third to the wind, and God will draw a sword after them. "A third part of you shall die of pestilence and be consumed with famine in your midst; a third part shall fall by the sword all around you; and a third part I will scatter to all the winds" (Ezekiel 5:12). This is not a metaphor reaching for an effect. This is a casualty count, divided and weighed out on a scale, and the people watching it are being shown their own funeral. The hair of the prophet is the population of the city, and most of it ends up in the fire, on the sword, or blown to the wind. God is doing arithmetic on a numb people who refused to do it themselves.

**The mercy of being made to see**
We would rather have the words. Words you can argue with, soften, file under interesting, walk away from unchanged. The siege acted out cannot be filed away, and that is the point. A people gets numb. They hear judgment described so many times that the description stops meaning anything, and the warning becomes background noise, and they sit inside a doomed city congratulating themselves on their stability. We do this. I have sat in rooms where everyone knew the marriage was over or the sin had taken root or the church was dying, and we all kept using calm, abstract, manageable words, because the calm words let us avoid the brick with the city scratched on it. The siege is no longer abstract precisely so that it can no longer be ignored.

And the sign-act points to a body still ahead. Centuries later God would make the sermon flesh again — not a prophet lying on his side rationing bread, but the Son himself, his body broken and his blood poured out, the judgment we earned acted out on a hill so that we could finally see what our sin actually costs and what love actually does to absorb it. Ezekiel's body bore the sign of the siege. Christ's body bore the siege itself. The mercy hidden inside this terrible chapter is that God refuses to let his people sleepwalk into the fire. He will scratch the city on a brick. He will shave the prophet's head. He will, in the end, give his own Son, rather than let us call the coming judgment abstract.

The judgment is no longer abstract.

## The Glory Departs
*The worship stayed; the presence left*

**Text:** Ezekiel 8–11 · **Supporting:** 1 Samuel 4:21–22; Jeremiah 7:4–11; Matthew 23:38; Romans 1:24

The most terrifying moment in the book of Ezekiel is not loud. It is the glory of God rising off the cherubim, pausing at the threshold, and going quietly out the east gate while the temple worship continues without noticing it is now an empty room.

**The idolatry behind the curtain**
In chapter eight the Spirit lifts Ezekiel by a lock of his hair and carries him in visions to Jerusalem, and God says, watch what they do here. There is an image of jealousy at the gate. There are seventy elders of Israel in a hidden chamber, each with his censer, in the dark, saying, "The LORD does not see us; the LORD has forsaken the land" (Ezekiel 8:12). There are women weeping for the foreign god Tammuz. There are men at the entrance of the temple, between the porch and the altar, with their backs to the sanctuary, bowing to the sun in the east. Layer after layer, and each one God calls a greater abomination than the last. The point is brutal and exact. The building still functioned. The sacrifices still smoked. And behind the curtain the leadership had decided God could not see, so they worshiped whatever they wanted in the dark. Jeremiah heard them chanting "the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD" like a charm while they stole and murdered and burned incense to Baal (Jeremiah 7:4–9). The shell was intact. The center had rotted.

**The slow leaving**
So the glory leaves, and Ezekiel watches it happen in slow motion, which is its own kind of horror. First the glory of God goes up from the cherub on which it rested to the threshold of the house (Ezekiel 9:3). Then "the glory of the LORD went out from the threshold of the house and stood over the cherubim" (Ezekiel 10:18). Then the cherubim lift their wings and mount up, and the glory of the God of Israel goes up from the midst of the city and stands on the mountain on the east side of the city (Ezekiel 11:23). Step by step, reluctant, lingering, pausing at every gate as if giving the city one more chance to notice — and the city does not notice. They had said the glory could never leave the temple. The whole nation was built on that certainty. And it left anyway, by the east gate, while the censers still swung. Israel had been here once before, when the ark was captured and a dying woman named her son Ichabod, "the glory has departed from Israel" (1 Samuel 4:21–22). They forgot. The presence is never owned. It is given.

**Ichabod over our own doors**
This is the judgment we never see coming, because it does not look like judgment. There is no fire, no army, no collapse on the day the glory leaves. The lights stay on. The service runs on time. The worship continues, polished and full and entirely empty, and everyone goes home satisfied, and not one of them felt the presence go. That is what should put us on our faces. We assume that because the building is full and the music is good and the brand is healthy, God is among us — when the most frightening sentence in all of Scripture might be Paul's quiet verdict that God, in judgment, "gave them up" (Romans 1:24), and Jesus' word over the temple of his own day, "your house is left to you desolate" (Matthew 23:38). I have led services that ran beautifully and wondered later whether God had been in the room at all, or whether I had mistaken competence for presence. The worst judgment is not God striking. It is God leaving, and letting the machine run on without him while we never miss him.

But hold on to the direction the glory went. It went east, and it stood on the mountain, and it waited — and this book does not end there. The same glory that left by the eastern gate will return by the eastern gate (Ezekiel 43). The presence that departs in judgment is the presence that will come back in mercy, and it came back finally in a man who is himself the glory of God dwelling among us, the true temple, who said tear this temple down and in three days I will raise it. The glory departed. But it was not done with this people, and it is not done with us. The terror of chapter ten is real. The east gate is not the last word.

The worst judgment is God leaving.

## The Soul That Sins
*The end of the excuse, the open door of the turn*

**Text:** Ezekiel 18:1–32 · **Supporting:** Jeremiah 31:29–30; Deuteronomy 24:16; 2 Peter 3:9; Luke 15:20

There was a proverb going around the exile community, and it was doing exactly what a good excuse always does. It explained the situation and it removed the responsibility, all in one tidy line.

**The proverb that blamed the dead**
"The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge" (Ezekiel 18:2). It sounds like wisdom. It sounds almost humble — we are suffering for what came before us, the system is rigged, the previous generation poisoned the well and we are only drinking what they left. And God will not let it stand. "As I live, declares the Lord GOD, this proverb shall no more be used by you in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine... the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:3–4). The whole chapter then works the case in three generations. A righteous man lives. His violent son dies for his own violence. That son's son, who sees his father's sin and does not imitate it, lives. Each one answers for himself. The Law had said this plainly — fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers (Deuteronomy 24:16) — and the people had buried it under a proverb that let them feel doomed instead of accountable. Fatalism is more comfortable than repentance. If it is all the fathers' fault, there is nothing to do but complain.

**The turn that goes both directions**
Then God says the thing that should change everything, and it cuts both ways at once. The wicked man who turns from all his sins and keeps God's statutes shall surely live; he shall not die, and none of the transgressions he committed shall be remembered against him (Ezekiel 18:21–22). And the righteous man who turns to injustice will die in it, and none of his former righteousness will be remembered (Ezekiel 18:24). No one is locked in by their past, in either direction. The sinner's record can be wiped. The saint's record cannot be coasted on. This is not a God grading on accumulated averages. This is a God who deals with you as you are, today, facing the direction you are facing now. And lest anyone hear in this a God who is cold or eager to condemn, the chapter gives us his own heart: "Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?" (Ezekiel 18:23). The God doing the judging does not want to do the burying.

**The door we keep blaming shut**
We are fluent in the sour-grapes proverb. We have a thousand versions of it. My father was like this. My church wounded me. My circumstances never gave me a chance. This is just how I am. And every one of those statements is sometimes a real description of a real injury — and every one of them can also become the proverb God outlawed, the line that converts a wound into a permanent excuse and locks the door from the inside while blaming someone else for locking it. I have done this with my own history. I have used a real absence to explain a chosen sin, and called it inevitable when God was calling it a choice I could turn from today. The mercy of this chapter is severe and it is enormous. Severe, because it takes the excuse away. Enormous, because the same move that removes the excuse opens the door. "Why will you die, O house of Israel? For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord GOD; so turn, and live" (Ezekiel 18:31–32).

And the turn this chapter commands is the turn the gospel makes possible. Peter says the Lord is patient toward us, not wishing that any should perish but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9) — the same heart, the same God. Jesus put a face on Ezekiel 18 when he told of a father who saw his ruined son still a long way off and ran (Luke 15:20). The wicked who turns will live, and none of his sins will be remembered — that is not just law, that is the cross, where the record was nailed and not held against the one who turns. The proverb said you are doomed by what came before. God says you are not. Turn around. The door is open and the Father is already running.

Turn, and live.

## The Shepherds Who Fed Themselves
*The owner is coming for his scattered sheep*

**Text:** Ezekiel 34:1–31 · **Supporting:** Jeremiah 23:1–4; John 10:11–16; 1 Peter 5:2–4; Psalm 23:1

God indicts the leaders before he rescues the sheep, and the order matters. The flock did not scatter by accident. It scattered because the men paid to guard it were busy eating it.

**The shepherds on trial**
"Ah, shepherds of Israel who have been feeding yourselves. Should not shepherds feed the sheep?" (Ezekiel 34:2). The charge sheet is specific and it is damning. You eat the fat, you clothe yourselves with the wool, you slaughter the fat ones, but you do not feed the sheep. The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the injured you have not bound up, the strayed you have not brought back, the lost you have not sought, and with force and harshness you have ruled them (Ezekiel 34:3–4). Every duty of a shepherd, listed by its omission. The men whose entire job was the welfare of the flock had inverted it — the flock now existed for the welfare of the men. And so the sheep were scattered over the mountains, food for every wild beast, with no one searching (Ezekiel 34:5–6). Jeremiah leveled the same charge: "Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture" (Jeremiah 23:1). The first thing God names is not the sheep's weakness. It is the shepherds' appetite.

**The owner takes the staff**
Then the announcement that turns the whole chapter, and it begins with two words that should terrify every leader and comfort every sheep: "Behold, I." "Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out" (Ezekiel 34:11). I will rescue them from all the places they have been scattered on a day of clouds and thick darkness. I will bring them out, gather them, feed them on the mountains, bind up the injured, strengthen the weak (Ezekiel 34:12–16). The hired men failed, so the owner is coming himself. And then, against every expectation, God says he will set one shepherd over them — "my servant David, and he shall feed them" (Ezekiel 34:23) — a coming king in the line of David who will be everything the false shepherds were not. The flock God will not lose. The leaders God will replace. The Shepherd God will send.

**The appetite in the man who feeds the flock**
It is easy to read this chapter as a sword aimed at someone else — the obvious wolf, the famous scandal, the leader caught fleecing the people. It is harder, and more honest, to feel the edge turn back. Any of us given charge of people — a pastor, a parent, an elder, anyone with sheep in their care — knows how quietly the inversion happens. You begin feeding the flock and you end up feeding on it, using the people for your sense of significance, your platform, your comfort, your need to be needed, while telling yourself it is all for them. I have stood in a pulpit and wondered whether I was feeding the sheep or feeding myself on their attention, and the line between the two is thinner than any shepherd wants to admit. The chapter does not let leaders off. Peter, who heard it firsthand, told elders to shepherd the flock "not for shameful gain, but eagerly... not domineering over those in your charge" (1 Peter 5:2–3). The shepherds who feed themselves are not only the obvious villains. On a bad week they are us.

Which is exactly why the gospel of this chapter is the best news a failed flock and a failing shepherd could hear. The one Shepherd God promised came and stood in front of religious leaders who fed themselves and said, "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep" (John 10:11). Not feeds on the sheep — feeds the sheep with his own body, and then lays down his life for them. He goes after the one that strayed. He knows his own and his own know him. The owner did come for his sheep, and the coming cost him everything, and that is the only thing that finally heals a flock scattered by men who loved themselves more than the lambs. The hirelings ran. The owner bled.

The owner is coming for his sheep.

## A New Heart and a New Spirit
*He gives the very thing he commands*

**Text:** Ezekiel 36:16–38 · **Supporting:** Jeremiah 31:31–34; Ezekiel 11:19–20; John 3:5–8; Titus 3:5

Of all the promises in this book, this is the one the New Testament cannot stop quoting, because it answers a question the whole Old Testament had been forcing us toward. What do you do with people who cannot keep the covenant even when they want to?

**Not because you deserve it**
First, God removes the one motive we would have assumed. He is going to act, but he is careful to say why, and the why is humbling. "It is not for your sake, O house of Israel, that I am about to act, but for the sake of my holy name, which you have profaned among the nations" (Ezekiel 36:22). Israel had been scattered for their sin, and in their scattering they had dragged God's reputation through the dirt among the nations who said, these are the LORD's people, and yet they had to leave his land. So God will act to vindicate his own name. This sounds at first like cold comfort — you are being saved not because you are loved but because God is protecting his reputation. But sit with it and it becomes the firmest ground there is. If God saved you because of something in you, your standing would be only as stable as you are. Because he saves for the sake of his own name, your salvation rests on something that cannot fail. Grace that depends on me is not grace. Grace that depends on his name is unbreakable.

**The heart of stone removed**
Then the promise itself, and it is the deepest diagnosis of the human problem in the Old Testament. The trouble was never only behavior. The trouble was the organ underneath the behavior. So God goes there: "I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean... And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. And I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes" (Ezekiel 36:25–27). Read those verbs and notice who does every one of them. I will sprinkle. I will give. I will remove. I will put. I will cause. Not one of them is a command to Israel. Every one is something God does to Israel. This is the same promise Jeremiah heard, the new covenant where God writes the law on the heart and remembers their sin no more (Jeremiah 31:33–34). The God who for centuries said walk in my statutes now says I will cause you to walk in them. The command finally comes with the power to obey it.

**The thing we cannot give ourselves**
We need to feel why this is the only good news there is, and it presses on something we would rather not admit. We believe, most of us, in a religion of effort — that if we are told the right things and try hard enough, we can produce the obedience God wants. And every honest person eventually meets the heart of stone in themselves, the thing that will not be argued or disciplined or willpowered into love for God, the gap between what we know we should want and what we actually want. I have preached harder effort to people whose problem was not effort but a stone heart, and I have driven myself the same way, as though the cure for a dead heart were a stricter to-do list. It never works, because you cannot will yourself a new will. The water has to be sprinkled on you. The stone has to be taken out. The Spirit has to be put in. Salvation is not God grading your attempt to change your heart. It is God doing the heart transplant you could never perform on yourself.

This is precisely what Jesus meant when he told a religious expert, a master of effort, that he must be born of water and the Spirit, born again from above (John 3:5–8) — Ezekiel 36 made personal. Paul says God saved us "not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit" (Titus 3:5). The new heart is not the reward for your obedience. It is the source of it, given before you could earn it, at the cross and by the Spirit. God commands a clean heart and a faithful walk — and then, astonishingly, he stoops down and gives the very thing he commanded. That is the whole gospel in one promise from the mouth of an exile by a canal.

He gives what he commands.

## The Valley of Dry Bones
*The word and the breath over a hopeless grave*

**Text:** Ezekiel 37:1–14 · **Supporting:** Genesis 2:7; Romans 4:17; John 11:43–44; Romans 8:11

God sets the prophet down in the worst possible place and asks the worst possible question, and the honest answer is no.

**Can these bones live**
The hand of the LORD carries Ezekiel out and sets him in the middle of a valley, and it is full of bones. He is led all around them, and two details land like blows. There were very many, and they were very dry (Ezekiel 37:2). Not freshly fallen soldiers. Not a battlefield with a hope of survivors. A valley of bones long dead, bleached, scattered, an army defeated so completely and so long ago that nothing of it remains but a field of dry bone. Then the question: "Son of man, can these bones live?" (Ezekiel 37:3). Every instinct says no. There is no more hopeless raw material in the world than dry bones. But Ezekiel has learned not to answer God's questions with his own arithmetic, so he says the thing that hands it back to God: "O Lord GOD, you know." He will not say no, because he has seen the wheels by the Chebar and knows this God deals in impossibilities. He will not say yes, because he is standing in a graveyard. He says, you know — and that is faith standing in the middle of the bones.

**The word, then the breath**
And God's method is the strange and beautiful center of the chapter. He does not simply raise them. He commands Ezekiel to prophesy — to preach to a field of bone. "Prophesy over these bones, and say to them, O dry bones, hear the word of the LORD" (Ezekiel 37:4). So he does, and there is a noise, a rattling, and the bones come together, bone to its bone, and sinews and flesh come up and skin covers them — but there is no breath in them (Ezekiel 37:7–8). Assembled corpses. A standing army with no life. Then the second command: prophesy to the breath, the ruach, the same word for wind and spirit, "Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live" (Ezekiel 37:9). And the breath comes, and they live, and stand on their feet, an exceedingly great army. The word reassembles. The breath makes alive. It is Genesis again, where God formed the man from dust and breathed into him the breath of life and the man became a living creature (Genesis 2:7). Creation, run a second time, over a graveyard.

**The people who said our hope is lost**
And then God tells Ezekiel what the bones mean, and it turns the vision from a wonder into a word for the despairing. "These bones are the whole house of Israel. Behold, they say, Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost; we are indeed cut off" (Ezekiel 37:11). The bones are the people, and the people have written their own epitaph. Our hope is lost. We are cut off. That is the sentence the exiles were saying to themselves by the rivers of Babylon, and it is the sentence we say in our own valleys — over a faith that feels long dead, a marriage that has gone to bone, a child far off, a part of ourselves we have already buried and stopped praying for. I have stood at the edge of situations and quietly agreed with the corpse, decided the bones were too dry and too many and too long gone, and stopped expecting anything. The God of this valley does not argue with our despair. He acts against it. He prophesies to it. He breathes on it.

This is the gospel pressing up through the floor of the Old Testament. The God here is the God Paul names, who "gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist" (Romans 4:17). It is the voice that stood outside a sealed tomb and shouted "Lazarus, come out," and the dead man walked out still wrapped in his graveclothes (John 11:43–44). It is the promise that the same Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead will give life to our mortal bodies (Romans 8:11). The valley is not the end of the story for a people who say their hope is lost, because the word still goes out over dry bones and the breath still comes from the four winds. You may be standing in a graveyard you have given up on. So was Ezekiel. Then God asked him a question and told him to start preaching to the dead.

These bones can live again.

## Gog and the End of the Threat
*No final enemy outlasts the people God secured*

**Text:** Ezekiel 38–39 · **Supporting:** Psalm 2:1–6; Revelation 20:7–9; Romans 8:31–39; Isaiah 54:17

After the dry bones stand up and the one Shepherd is set over the gathered flock, a reader might still carry one fear. Granted God can restore his people — but can he keep them? What about the next threat, the enemy still out there beyond the horizon? Chapters 38 and 39 exist to answer exactly that fear.

**The enemy summoned and defeated**
Gog, of the land of Magog, is the menace from the far north, the coalition of distant nations, the picture of the ultimate hostile power gathering against God's restored and unsuspecting people. They are living in safety, in unwalled villages, at rest, when this great horde comes up like a cloud covering the land (Ezekiel 38:8–11). And the terror of it lasts only as long as it takes to read who is actually in control. "I will turn you about and put hooks into your jaws, and I will bring you out" (Ezekiel 38:4). God summons the enemy. The threat that looks like it has the initiative is on a hook held by the God it came to destroy. And when Gog finally comes against the land, God himself acts — "my wrath will be roused in my anger... I will summon a sword against Gog" — and the great horde falls on the mountains of Israel, food for the birds, buried for seven months, weapons burned for seven years (Ezekiel 39:4, 9–12). The most fearsome enemy in the book is dispatched in a sentence and cleaned up for years. The threat was never a real contest.

**For the sake of the name, again**
And notice why God does it, because it is the same reason that drove chapter 36. This is not about Israel's military strength or their deserving. "I will set my glory among the nations, and all the nations shall see my judgment... So I will show my greatness and my holiness and make myself known in the eyes of many nations. Then they will know that I am the LORD" (Ezekiel 38:23, 39:7). The defeat of Gog is the vindication of God's name in front of the whole watching world. This is the same truth the second Psalm sings — the nations rage and the kings take counsel together against the LORD, and the One enthroned in heaven laughs, and sets his King on the holy hill (Psalm 2:1–6). The raging of the final enemy is real, but it is not a threat to God's purpose. It is the stage on which God displays that no power can undo what he has secured for his name and his flock.

**The fear that outlives our faith**
We need this chapter because restoration alone does not cure our anxiety. We can believe God forgave us, gave us a new heart, raised our dead places — and still lie awake certain that something out there is finally going to take it all back. The diagnosis we never overcame. The collapse waiting around the corner. The enemy, named or unnamed, that we are sure is stronger than the grace that found us. I have done this. I have trusted God for the rescue and then spent my strength bracing for the relapse, as though the God who raised the dry bones could be outmuscled by whatever I feared most. Gog answers that. The final threat is real, it gathers, it covers the land like a cloud — and God puts a hook in its jaw. Our security was never our ability to fend off the last enemy. It was always the name of the God who secured us.

And the New Testament tells us the last enemy by name. Revelation borrows this very scene — Gog and Magog gathered for the final assault, and fire comes down from heaven and consumes them (Revelation 20:7–9) — to say that the last rebellion ends the way this one does, in a moment, with no contest. Paul presses it all the way home: if God is for us, who can be against us, and neither death nor life nor things present nor things to come nor any power will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:31–39). No weapon formed against you shall prosper (Isaiah 54:17). The enemy you are bracing for has a hook in its jaw. The God who found you in exile and gave you a new heart and raised your dry bones is not going to lose you to the last threat on the horizon. He summoned it. He ends it.

No enemy outlasts God's people.

## The Glory Returns to the Temple
*The presence that departed in judgment comes back to dwell*

**Text:** Ezekiel 40–43 · **Supporting:** Ezekiel 10:18–19; Haggai 2:6–9; John 1:14; Revelation 21:3

If you have walked through this whole book, you have been carrying a wound since chapter ten. You watched the glory leave. You watched it rise off the cherubim and pause at the threshold and go out the east gate while the worship continued, oblivious. That wound is what chapters 40 through 43 were written to heal.

**The measured house**
The vision is patient to the point of tedium, and the tedium is the point. A man with a measuring line of bronze takes Ezekiel through a new temple and measures everything — the gates, the walls, the chambers, the courts, the thresholds, cubit by cubit, for three long chapters. Why all the measuring? Because measurement is permanence. You do not survey a tent you intend to fold up tomorrow. The exhaustive, careful, dimensioned house is God saying, this is not provisional. This is built to stand. After a book full of judgment acted out on the prophet's body and a city reduced to a third in the fire and a third on the sword, God answers with a building so precisely measured it cannot be mistaken for a temporary mercy. The detail is the promise. He is settling in.

**The glory comes back the way it left**
And then, after all the measuring, the moment the whole book has been waiting for. "And behold, the glory of the God of Israel was coming from the east. And the sound of his coming was like the sound of many waters, and the earth shone with his glory" (Ezekiel 43:2). From the east. The exact direction it left. The glory that went out the eastern gate and stood on the mountain on the east side of the city now returns from the east, by the same road, and Ezekiel — who watched it go — watches it come back. "As the glory of the LORD entered the temple by the gate facing east... the glory of the LORD filled the temple" (Ezekiel 43:4–5). And the voice from inside the house says, "Son of man, this is the place of my throne... where I will dwell in the midst of the people of Israel forever" (Ezekiel 43:7). The departure of chapter ten is undone, gate for gate, direction for direction, and this time the word attached to the presence is forever. Haggai would later promise that the glory of this latter house would be greater than the former, and that in this place God would give peace (Haggai 2:9). The presence is not just back. It is back to stay.

**The return we keep doubting**
We carry the chapter-ten wound in our own histories. We have known the felt presence of God and then known its absence — a season when prayer was alive and then a season of silence, a faith that burned and then went cold, a time we walked closely with him and then a long stretch where the house felt empty and we wondered if the glory had gone out some eastern gate while we were not watching. And the lie we believe in that stretch is that the leaving is the last word — that what departed is gone for good, that the presence we lost is not coming back. I have lived in that stretch and quietly concluded the best of God was behind me. This vision will not allow that conclusion. The glory that departs in judgment is the glory that returns in mercy, by the same gate, to a house measured for permanence, to dwell forever. God's leaving is never his final act with a people he means to keep.

And we know now where this return finally landed. The glory that filled this measured temple was pointing past itself to the day when the Word became flesh and dwelt — literally, tabernacled — among us, and we beheld his glory (John 1:14). The presence came back not in a building but in a person, Immanuel, God with us, the true temple. And the last vision of all of Scripture takes Ezekiel's promise and makes it the end of the whole story: a loud voice from the throne saying, "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his God" (Revelation 21:3). The glory that left by the eastern gate did not abandon this people. It was always coming back. It came back in Christ, and it is coming back to fill everything, forever.

The glory that left returns.

## The River and the Name of the City
*From under the threshold, a river that heals everything it touches*

**Text:** Ezekiel 47–48 · **Supporting:** Genesis 2:10; John 7:37–39; Revelation 22:1–5; Psalm 46:4

The book that began with the glory leaving ends with a river rising, and the last word of the whole vision is a name — the name that resolves everything Ezekiel has seen.

**The river that should not deepen**
It starts as a trickle. Water issues from below the threshold of the temple, from under the place where the glory now dwells, and flows east. The guide leads Ezekiel out and measures a thousand cubits and has him wade through — ankle-deep. Another thousand — knee-deep. Another thousand — waist-deep. Another thousand, "and it was a river that I could not pass through, for the water had risen... a river that could not be passed through" (Ezekiel 47:5). This is not how rivers behave. A river without tributaries thins as it travels; this one deepens with no stream feeding it, growing the farther it gets from its source, because its source is not rainfall but the presence of God under the threshold. And everywhere it goes it brings life: "wherever the river goes, every living creature that swarms will live... everything will live where the river goes" (Ezekiel 47:9). It pours into the Dead Sea — the saltiest, most lifeless water in the world — and the waters become fresh and fill with fish. On its banks grow trees whose leaves do not wither and whose fruit does not fail, fruit for food and leaves for healing (Ezekiel 47:12). The presence of God turns even the Dead Sea into a fishery.

**The name that ends the book**
And then the long allotment of the land among the tribes, the careful portioning of an inheritance to a people who had lost everything, and the city laid out with its gates named for the tribes. And the final verse of the entire book, the last word after fifty chapters that began with deportation and idolatry and departing glory and dry bones, is a name given to the city: "And the name of the city from that time on shall be, The LORD Is There" (Ezekiel 48:35). Yahweh Shammah. The LORD is there. That is the resolution of the whole vision. The glory that left the city in chapter ten has so completely returned that the city's very name is now the announcement of his presence. Not the LORD was there. Not the LORD might return. The LORD is there — present tense, permanent, the defining fact about the place. Everything the book grieved is answered in three words on a city gate.

**The river we keep mistaking for a trickle**
We are tempted to measure the work of God by how it starts, and it almost always starts ankle-deep. A trickle of grace under the threshold of a life. A small turning, a first prayer, a faith that feels too thin to hold any weight, a healing that begins so quietly we are not sure it is real. And because it starts small we write it off, or we stand in the shallows and conclude this is all there will be. I have done that — measured God's work in someone, or in myself, by the ankle-deep beginning and stopped wading before it could rise. But this river deepens the farther it runs from its source, because the source is inexhaustible. The God whose presence under the threshold turns the Dead Sea fresh is not going to leave you in the shallows. What looks like a trickle is a river you will not be able to cross.

And we know now where this river runs. The river that flowed from Eden to water the garden (Genesis 2:10) flows again here from the temple, and Jesus stood up in the temple and cried out that whoever believes in him will have rivers of living water flow out of him — and John tells us he meant the Spirit (John 7:37–39). The presence under the threshold is the Spirit poured out, deepening with every thousand cubits, healing every dead place it reaches. And the last pages of Scripture take this exact vision and complete it: a river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, with the tree of life on its banks whose leaves are for the healing of the nations, and no more curse, and his servants will see his face (Revelation 22:1–5). The book that opened with the glory departing closes with a name on a gate, and the name is the gospel itself, and the end of the whole story. God with us. The LORD is there.

The LORD is there.
